then.text: A full book, and the Hairy Hands on top. That's a story for the Postbridge pub. Mind how you go on the B3212.
You did what? You caught the Hairy Hands? On the B3212? Well I never. That's one stamp nobody else has got.
Here. My old Turned Coat badge. Old Devon folk turned their coats inside out if the pixies led them astray on the moor. It works. Mostly.
All three! Cranmere and all. Now, there's one more, if you've the nerve. They say there's a stamp you only get after dark, on this road.
The Hairy Hands. Big, hairy and grabby, on the B3212 by the moor. Go and see, at night, if you dare. I won't. I'm driving.
The oaks in the boulders, south-west of here. Haldon, by the Belvedere. And Cranmere Pool, up on the north moor. Happy hunting.

else.text: {greeting} Letterboxing! Ever done it? You hunt for little boxes hidden on the moor, with a clue and a compass. Inside: a rubber stamp and a visitors' book.

You stamp your book with the box's stamp, and the box's book with your own. It began in 1854, when a Dartmoor guide called James Perrott left a bottle at Cranmere Pool for walkers to leave their calling cards in.
Fancy a go? There are three I like: one in the stunted oaks, one up by the Belvedere on Haldon, and the oldest of all, at Cranmere Pool, way up on the north moor.

then.text: There's a stamp book for you. Off you go, and remember the code: put the box back exactly as you found it.

else.text: Fair enough. The boxes have been there since before you were born, mostly.

then.text: You've got this one already. Put it back nice and snug, mind.

You found it! Under the third rock from the oak, in an old sandwich tin. This one's in the oaks, so the stamp's a wisht old tree. The real Wistman's Wood is high on the moor; these oaks are its cousins.
You press the box's stamp on to a fresh page of your book: a twisted oak with a face in the bark.

else.text: Letterboxing? Lovely hobby. Fresh air, a good map, and the thrill of finding a sandwich tin. You'll want a stamp book from the letterboxer on the B3212 first. And this one's best done first.

then.text: You've got this one already. Put it back nice and snug, mind.

You found it! Under the third rock from the oak, in an old sandwich tin. Up here you can see the moor one way and the sea the other. The Belvedere was built for a friend, which is nicer than most towers.
You press the box's stamp on to a fresh page of your book: the Belvedere, three turrets and a flag.

else.text: Letterboxing? Lovely hobby. Fresh air, a good map, and the thrill of finding a sandwich tin. You'll want a stamp book from the letterboxer on the B3212 first. And find the one in the oaks before mine, it's tradition.

then.text: Out of the dark at the edge of the road come two great hands, grey-haired to the knuckle, flexing slowly. They have been waiting.

else.text: The road is empty and the moor is black. Then the hedge at the verge rustles, and two huge hands crawl out on their fingertips, like crabs.
They are covered in coarse dark hair. There is no arm, no body, nothing. Just hands, and the feeling that they would very much like to hold something. A steering wheel. Your shoulder.

then.text: The Hairy Hands settle into the snare, folded neatly, like a pair of gloves left on a seat. One of them gives a little wave.

else.text: The hands scuttle back into the hedge. Somewhere down the road, a cattle grid rattles though nothing crossed it.
A lay-by on the B3212. Tyre marks swerve off the tarmac and on to the verge, then back again, as if someone was pushed. Nothing here by daylight. Best come back after dark.

then.text: She's burning. From up here they'd see it in Exeter, and the next beacon east would take it on. Go on, to the city. Find the Town Crier.
Smoke over Plymouth way, you say? And the Hoe beacon's lit? Then it's real!
The keeper thrusts a torch into the iron basket. Tarred wood crackles, and flame leaps up into the wind off the sea.
Now get down to Exeter, quick as you like. The Town Crier's on the High Street. He'll raise the city.

else.text: This is the Haldon beacon. One of a chain of fires on high ground, ready to send a warning from the coast to the city in less time than a horse could gallop it.
Nobody's needed it since 1588. I keep it dry anyway. You never know with the Spanish. Or the weather.

est_warden.text: Avocets! There, on the mud. Black and white, legs like knitting needles, and a bill that curves up at the end. They sweep it side to side through the mud for shrimps and worms.
In winter we get one of the biggest flocks in the country here. And Brent geese from Siberia, thousands of them, muttering. Bring a flask. Bring two.

est_pumper.text: Brunel's atmospheric railway. No locomotive. Engines in pumping houses like this sucked the air out of a pipe laid between the rails, and a piston under the train got pushed along by the air behind it.
Quiet, smooth, quick. But the pipe was sealed with greased leather, and the leather perished in the salt air. People say rats ate it. It lasted less than a year. Brilliant idea, wrong century.

est_pixie_gran.text: {greeting} I'm from Ottery St Mary, over the river. Every June we have Pixie Day. The children dress up as pixies and capture the bell ringers.

The story goes the pixies didn't want church bells in Ottery and tried to kidnap the ringers. The bells won, and the pixies were banished to a cave by the river, Pixies' Parlour. They come back once a year. With face paint.
If they lead you astray on the moor, turn your coat inside out. Confuses them no end.

poole_marshal.text: Road's shut for the Harbour Regatta marshals' briefing. We're only letting through trainers who've won the Storm Stone at Cardiff. It's safety, apparently. Or a bit of a lark.
Come back when you've got it, and we'll wave you through with a flag.

landsky_beavers.text: Shh. Dusk is when they come out. No, not here, up on the River Otter, past Budleigh. But I practise.

Beavers were hunted out of Britain about five hundred years ago, for the fur and for a gland they use in perfume. Then in 2014 a family turned up on the Otter. Nobody will say how. Devon Wildlife Trust got a five-year trial licence in 2015, and in 2020 the government said they could stay: the first wild beavers allowed in England in centuries.

They're engineers. The dams slow a flood, hold water back in a drought, and make pools where kingfishers, frogs and dragonflies move in. Scotland has had them since the Knapdale trial in 2009, and protected them by law in 2019. In 2025 England began licensing wild releases too.
Rewilding isn't putting the clock back. It's handing the land a few of its old tools and watching what it builds. Beavers, cattle, storks, bogs. Mostly bogs, round my way.
